mcqs.question: Why does sorting by finish time (rather than start time or duration) make the greedy activity-selection strategy correct?
options: Finish time is always numerically smaller than start time, simplifying the sort
Taking the earliest-finishing compatible activity always leaves the maximum possible remaining time for whatever comes after, regardless of that activity's own start time or length
Sorting by finish time makes the algorithm run in O(n) instead of O(n log n)
Finish time sorting only works when all activities have the same duration
mcqs.explanation: The earliest-finishing compatible option maximizes the remaining time window for subsequent choices, which is the structural property the correctness proof relies on. Start time or duration alone don't guarantee this — an early-starting or short activity can still occupy a slot that blocks more total activities than a differently-timed one would.

mcqs.question: Why does sorting by duration (shortest activity first) fail as a greedy strategy for activity selection?
options: Sorting by duration is actually equivalent to sorting by finish time in every case
It fails only when two activities have exactly the same duration
A short activity can still occupy an awkward time slot that blocks two other activities on either side, when a different choice would have let both through
Duration-based sorting is correct, but slower than finish-time sorting
mcqs.explanation: A short activity's placement in time (not just its length) determines what it blocks — it can sit in a spot that conflicts with two otherwise-compatible longer activities, producing a worse total count than choosing based on finish time would.

mcqs.question: An activity ends at time 5 and another starts at time 5. Are they compatible in activity selection?
options: Always incompatible, since they share the exact same time value
Always compatible, this is a universal rule for all interval problems
It depends entirely on the specific problem's definition of overlap (closed vs. half-open intervals) — this must be confirmed, not assumed
Compatibility at this boundary never affects the final answer
mcqs.explanation: Whether touching endpoints count as overlapping is a convention the problem statement defines, and different formulations (closed intervals vs. half-open ones) answer it differently. Assuming one convention without checking can silently shift the final count by one activity.

mcqs.question: Weighted activity selection adds a value to each activity and asks to maximize total value instead of count. Why does the greedy finish-time strategy no longer apply?
options: Weighted activity selection is unsolvable by any algorithm
The greedy strategy still applies unchanged; only the final count needs to be multiplied by the weights afterward
Sorting by weight instead of finish time fixes the problem while keeping the rest of the algorithm the same

A high-value activity overlapping several lower-value ones might be worth choosing over all of them combined — finishing earliest says nothing about value, so the greedy-choice property no longer holds
mcqs.explanation: Once value enters the picture, 'finishes earliest' no longer guarantees the locally best choice is part of the optimal solution — a single overlapping high-value activity can legitimately beat several lower-value non-overlapping ones. This breaks the greedy-choice property, which is exactly why the weighted variant needs a DP formulation instead.
